REAL EARNINGS  OCTOBER 2026 
All employees 
Real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September to October, seasonally 
adjusted, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. This result stems from an increase of 0.4 
percent in average hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.4 percent in the Consumer Price 
Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). 
Real average weekly earnings were unchanged over the month due to no change in real average hourly 
earnings combined with no change in the average workweek. 
******************************************************************************************************** 
* Federal Government Shutdown * 
* * 
* This release usually includes an over-the-year analysis of changes to real earnings. BLS could not * 
* collect the relevant Consumer Price Index data for the October 2025 reference period due to a lapse * 
* in appropriations in late 2025. For that reason, over-the-year comparisons from October 2025 to * 
* October 2026 are not available. * 
* * 
******************************************************************************************************** 
Production and nonsupervisory employees 
Real average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory employees increased 0.1 percent from 
September to October, seasonally adjusted. This result stems from a 0.4-percent increase in average 
hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.3 percent in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage 
Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). 
Real average weekly earnings decreased 0.3 percent over the month due to the change in real average 
hourly earnings combined with a decrease of 0.3 percent in the average workweek. 
___________ 
The Real Earnings news release for November 2026 is scheduled to be published on Thursday, 
December 10, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. (ET).

 November 12, 2026 
EIA forecasts Alaskan crude oil production to grow 13% in 2027 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook, November 2026 
After decades of decline, crude oil production in Alaska is growing, driven by two projects on Alaska’s North Slope. In our latest Short-Term Energy Outlook, we expect a 23,000 barrels per day (b/d) (6%) increase in 2026, followed by a 60,000 b/d (13%) rise in 2027. At a forecast 505,000 b/d in 2027, output would be the most since 2014. 
If realized, these annual production increases will be the largest since the 1980s, when Alaskan crude production peaked at 2.0 million b/d. 
The recent growth is attributable to two projects on Alaska's North Slope: 
The Nuna project, owned by ConocoPhillips, started production in December 2024 and is expected to produce 20,000 b/d at its peak. So far this year, it has produced an average of 10,000 b/d, partially offsetting existing production declines. 
The Pikka Phase 1 project, jointly owned by Santos and Repsol, began production in May 2026 with initial average monthly production of 2,000 b/d and reaching 38,000 b/d as of September 2026, according to data from the Alaska Oil & Gas Conservation Commission. We expect peak production of 80,000 b/d by winter 2026–27, nearly 20% of total Alaskan production in 2025. 
Notably, our STEO production data indicate that third-quarter 2026 production grew 4% as Pikka Phase 1 came online, marking the first third-quarter production increase in more than 40 years. Alaskan crude output typically dips in late summer when operators conduct annual maintenance, running an average of 7% lower than first-quarter levels over the previous five years (2021–2025). 
Principal contributor: Trinity Manning-Pickett

Explanatory Notes
Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.
For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.
Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.
Revision procedure (Census basis)
Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau revises the aggregate seasonally adjusted (nominal and real, or chained-dollar) and unadjusted export, import, and trade balance figures, as well as the end-use totals for the prior month. Country detail data and commodity detail data, based on the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC) Revision 4 and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), are not revised monthly. The timing adjustment shown in exhibit 14 is the difference between monthly data as originally reported and as recompiled.
For August 2026, unadjusted exports of goods were revised up $0.1 billion and unadjusted imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion. Goods carry-over in September 2026 was $0.8 billion (0.4 percent) for exports and $0.4 billion (0.1 percent) for imports. For August 2026, revised export carry-over was less than $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent) and revised import carry-over was $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent).
Quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollar series: For March, June, September, and December statistical month releases, revisions are made to the real, or chained-dollar, series presented in exhibits 10 and 11: the previous five months are revised to incorporate the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) revisions to price indexes, which are used to produce the real series and to align Census data with data published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the national income and product accounts (NIPAs).
Annual revisions: Each June, not seasonally adjusted goods data are revised to redistribute monthly data that arrived too late for inclusion in the month of transaction. EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EDT, Thursday, October 29, 2026
 BEA 26—45
GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, compared with an increase of 5.0 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent.

The full release schedule for 2027 is available on BEA's website.
Technical Notes
Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

Personal Income and Outlays, September 2026
Personal income increased $54.5 billion (0.2 percent at a monthly rate) in September, according to estimates released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). Disposable personal income (DPI)—personal income less personal current taxes—increased $52.7 billion (0.2 percent), and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $113.1 billion (0.5 percent).
Personal outlays—the sum of PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments—increased $113.0 billion in September. Personal saving was $911.1 billion, and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of DPI—was 3.8 percent.
The increase in current-dollar personal income in September primarily reflected increases in compensation and government social benefits.
The $113.1 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in September reflected increases of $35.1 billion in spending on goods and $78.1 billion in spending on services.
Real PCE increased $2.6 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in September.
From the preceding month, the PCE price index for September increased 0.5 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.3 percent.
From the same month one year ago, the PCE price index for September increased 3.6 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 3.1 percent from one year ago.

 November 17, 2026 
How does EIA account for small differences between energy supply and demand data? 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
Note: Supply = production + imports; demand = consumption + exports; demand - supply = stock change + other 
EIA uses over 60 surveys to collect data on the U.S. energy sector’s supply and demand. In theory, supply and demand should balance. In practice, we often have small differences between our total supply and total demand figures. 
To account for the differences between U.S. total primary energy supply and demand, our Monthly Energy Review includes a stock change and other data series, a grouping of items that account for the differences between supply and demand each month. 
These accounting differences represent a very small share of energy markets. In 2025, our combined surveys accounted for about 128 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) each for U.S. energy supply and demand, and stock change and other was 0.4 quads—about 0.3% of the total. 
Stock change is the net difference between energy held in storage at the beginning and end of a month. 
The other portion of stock change and other represents the many forms of small accounting differences: 
Differences in survey respondent accounting and reporting practices 
Differences in timing between energy activity occurrences and reporting periods 
Measurement and estimation errors 
Limitations in data collection systems and survey coverage 
Energy lost during transfers or storage 
Unreported energy activities 
To document the other differences between supply and demand, besides stock change, we use various adjustments, balancing items, and losses and unaccounted for series, a standard statistical accounting practice. Rather than indicating a flaw in the underlying statistics, these series ensure that published data are consistent and transparent, while also providing a measure of the uncertainty associated with our survey data. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review
For petroleum and biofuels, our adjustments series accounts for the fact that survey responses may not precisely reflect actual activity. We’ve made improvements to our petroleum data over time to account for changes in transfers to crude oil supply, motor gasoline blending components, distillate fuel oil by pipeline operations, and other developments in petroleum markets. See Appendix B of our Petroleum Supply Monthly for more details. 
For natural gas, our balancing item series accounts for differences between supply and demand. Some of the differences are because of natural gas lost to the atmosphere. Also, there can be differences in conversions of flow data metered at varying temperatures and pressures, variations in company accounting and billing practices, and differences between billing cycles and calendar periods. See Appendix A of our Natural Gas Monthly for more details. 
For coal, we use a losses and unaccounted for series to represent differences in supply and demand, including coal lost during transport and various accounting and timing issues. In 2009, because of incomplete data coverage and different source data, biofuels have a small balancing item to balance biodiesel supply and demand. 
Principal contributors: Allen McFarland, Mickey Francis

 November 13, 2026 
Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data 
Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey. 
Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. 
To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows. 
However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook, November 2026 
We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. 
According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.
